title: Summarize Evolving Use Cases for Modern Network Environments

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Modern networks are becoming more software-driven, automated, policy-based, cloud-connected, and identity-aware while relying less on manual device-by-device configuration. This objective connects programmable networking, overlays, zero trust, cloud-delivered security, infrastructure as code, source control, and IPv6 transition.
bullets: Software-defined networking (SDN) and software-defined wide area networking (SD-WAN)
Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) and Security Service Edge (SSE)
sections.callout: Centralize → automate → segment → verify → secure → version → modernize addressing.

sections.title: Maestro Focus

sections.title: SDN and SD-WAN

entries.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
paragraphs: SDN separates network control logic from the individual devices that forward traffic. Instead of configuring each device independently, administrators gain centralized and programmable control.
entries.recognitionCue: Network behavior is centrally controlled through software rather than configured independently on every device → SDN.

entries.title: Software-Defined Wide Area Network (SD-WAN)
paragraphs: SD-WAN applies software-defined control specifically to wide area network connectivity. It can centrally manage branch traffic across broadband, MPLS, cellular, Internet links, and other transports.
entries.recognitionCue: An organization centrally manages branch WAN connectivity using software → SD-WAN.

sections.callout: SDN is broad software-defined network control; SD-WAN focuses on WAN connectivity.

entries.title: Application-Aware Networking
paragraphs: An application-aware SD-WAN identifies traffic by application and makes routing or policy decisions accordingly. Voice traffic can use one path while bulk backup traffic uses another.
entries.memoryHook: What application is this traffic from?
entries.recognitionCue: The WAN path is selected according to application type → Application-aware SD-WAN.

entries.title: Zero-Touch Provisioning
paragraphs: Zero-touch provisioning deploys equipment with little or no manual configuration at the remote site. The device connects to the network, contacts its management system, downloads configuration, and applies policy.
entries.memoryHook: Plug it in and it configures itself.
entries.recognitionCue: A branch device arrives with no local network engineer required → Zero-touch provisioning.

entries.title: Transport Agnostic
paragraphs: A transport-agnostic system applies policy across different underlying connection types, including broadband, fiber, MPLS, and cellular.
entries.memoryHook: The underlay can change; policy still works.
entries.recognitionCue: SD-WAN operates across multiple carrier technologies → Transport agnostic.

entries.title: Central Policy Management
paragraphs: Administrators define network rules once from a centralized control system and apply them across many devices or sites, reducing repetitive configuration.
entries.memoryHook: One policy → many devices and sites.
entries.recognitionCue: An administrator changes branch routing or security policy from one platform → Central policy management.

entries.title: Virtual Extensible Local Area Network (VXLAN)
paragraphs: VXLAN creates Layer 2 overlay networks across Layer 3 infrastructure. It lets logically connected Layer 2 networks extend across routed infrastructure in data centers, virtualized environments, and large-scale networks.
entries.recognitionCue: A Layer 2 network must extend across a Layer 3 data-center fabric → VXLAN.

entries.title: Layer 2 Encapsulation
paragraphs: VXLAN encapsulates Layer 2 Ethernet traffic so it can travel across a Layer 3 IP network. Systems can appear to share one logical Layer 2 segment even when the physical path is routed.
entries.recognitionCue: Ethernet traffic is carried across an IP underlay → VXLAN encapsulation.

entries.title: Data Center Interconnect (DCI)
paragraphs: DCI connects separate data-center environments. VXLAN can support designs that extend logical Layer 2 networks between data centers.
entries.recognitionCue: Workloads in separate data centers need logically connected network segments → DCI.

sections.title: Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA)
paragraphs: ZTA does not automatically trust users, devices, or connections merely because they are inside a network. Trust is evaluated per request using policy and context.

entries.title: Policy-Based Authentication
paragraphs: Authentication answers who you are. In a Zero Trust environment, policy can evaluate user identity, device, location, risk, and authentication method.

entries.title: Authorization
paragraphs: Authorization answers what an authenticated user or system is allowed to do. Authentication comes first; authorization determines access afterward.

entries.title: Least Privilege Access
paragraphs: Users and systems receive only the access required to perform their tasks and nothing more.
entries.recognitionCue: An employee needs read-only access to one application and nothing else → Least privilege.

sections.callout: Verify identity → check policy → authorize → grant minimum access. Trust is earned per request, not assumed by location.

sections.title: SASE and SSE

entries.title: Secure Access Service Edge (SASE)
paragraphs: SASE combines networking and security capabilities in a cloud-delivered architecture for remote users, cloud applications, and traffic that may not traverse a traditional headquarters perimeter.
examples: Traffic outside a traditional headquarters perimeter
entries.memoryHook: Networking + security at the edge or cloud.
entries.recognitionCue: An organization combines WAN access and cloud-delivered security controls → SASE.

entries.title: Security Service Edge (SSE)
paragraphs: SSE focuses on the security-services portion of SASE without the complete WAN networking component.
entries.memoryHook: SASE security without the WAN piece.
entries.recognitionCue: The scenario requests cloud-delivered security services rather than WAN connectivity → SSE.

sections.callout: SASE includes networking and security; SSE focuses on security services.

sections.title: Infrastructure as Code (IaC)
paragraphs: IaC defines and manages infrastructure through code or structured configuration files instead of relying on manual device-by-device changes. It improves repeatability, consistency, speed, version tracking, and resistance to manual error.

entries.title: Playbooks, Templates, and Reusable Tasks
paragraphs: A playbook defines a series of automated actions, a template provides a reusable configuration structure, and a reusable task performs an operation that can be invoked repeatedly.
entries.recognitionCue: Fifty switches receive the same automated instructions → Playbook or template automation.

entries.title: Configuration Drift and Compliance
paragraphs: Configuration drift occurs when actual configuration no longer matches the intended or approved state. Automation can detect drift, restore the desired state, and verify compliance.
examples: Approved: SSH enabled and Telnet disabled
Compliance: automation detects and corrects the mismatch

entries.title: Automated Upgrades
paragraphs: Automation can coordinate consistent upgrades across many devices, reducing repetitive work. Upgrades still require testing and proper change-management controls.

entries.title: Dynamic Inventories
paragraphs: A dynamic inventory automatically discovers or updates the systems that automation should manage as devices appear, disappear, scale, or change addresses.
entries.recognitionCue: The automation platform discovers which current systems need configuration → Dynamic inventory.

sections.title: Source Control
paragraphs: IaC configuration belongs in source control so teams can track changes, versions, contributors, conflicts, and parallel work with software-development discipline.

entries.title: Version Control
paragraphs: Version control tracks changes over time and supports history, rollback, auditing, and comparison.
entries.recognitionCue: An administrator needs a previous network-configuration version → Version control.

entries.title: Central Repository
paragraphs: A central repository stores the authoritative shared code and configuration so team members can retrieve and contribute changes.

entries.title: Conflict Identification
paragraphs: A conflict occurs when incompatible changes affect the same code or configuration. Source control identifies the collision so it can be resolved.

entries.title: Branching
paragraphs: A branch creates an independent line of development. An engineer can prepare a new VLAN configuration separately from production, test it, and merge it only when ready.
entries.memoryHook: Work on a change without altering the main version yet.
entries.recognitionCue: An engineer develops configuration separately from production → Branching.

sections.title: IPv6 Addressing
paragraphs: IPv4 uses 32-bit addressing. IPv6 uses 128-bit addressing and a vastly larger address space. IPv6 mitigates IPv4 address exhaustion. During migration, networks must account for systems and services that still require IPv4 compatibility.
sections.callout: IPv6 expands addressing; transition methods maintain compatibility during coexistence.

entries.title: Tunneling
paragraphs: Tunneling encapsulates IPv6 traffic so it can cross IPv4-only infrastructure.
entries.recognitionCue: IPv6 islands must communicate across an IPv4-only network → Tunneling.

entries.title: Dual Stack
paragraphs: A dual-stack device or network runs IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously and selects the appropriate protocol according to the destination and available support.
entries.recognitionCue: A server has both IPv4 and IPv6 configured → Dual stack.

entries.title: NAT64
paragraphs: NAT64 uses protocol and address translation so IPv6-only systems can communicate with IPv4 systems.
entries.recognitionCue: An IPv6-only client must reach an IPv4-only server → NAT64.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Traffic decisions based on application → Application aware
Multiple WAN transport types → Transport agnostic
One place defines WAN policy → Central policy management
Ethernet carried through a routed network → Layer 2 encapsulation
Networking plus security as a cloud service → SASE
Actual configuration differs from intended → Configuration drift
IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously → Dual stack

entries.title: SDN vs. SD-WAN
paragraphs: SDN is broad software-defined network control; SD-WAN focuses on wide-area connectivity.

entries.title: Zero-Touch Provisioning vs. Central Policy Management
paragraphs: Zero-touch provisioning deploys a device without local manual setup. Central policy management changes policy from one control point.

entries.title: SASE vs. SSE
paragraphs: SASE combines networking and security. SSE focuses on the cloud-delivered security functions.

entries.title: VXLAN vs. Ordinary VLAN
paragraphs: VXLAN carries a Layer 2 overlay across Layer 3 infrastructure; an ordinary VLAN remains a local Layer 2 segmentation concept.

entries.title: Authentication vs. Authorization
paragraphs: Authentication verifies identity. Authorization determines permitted resources and actions.

entries.title: ZTA vs. Least Privilege
paragraphs: ZTA is the broader architecture of continuous verification and policy-based access. Least privilege is the principle of granting only required permissions within that architecture.

entries.title: Configuration Drift vs. Version Control
paragraphs: Configuration drift means the actual system differs from the desired state. Version control tracks file and configuration revisions over time.

entries.title: Repository vs. Branch
paragraphs: A repository is the central shared storage for code and configuration. A branch is an independent line of development within that work.

entries.title: Tunneling vs. Dual Stack vs. NAT64
paragraphs: Tunneling encapsulates, dual stack runs both protocols, and NAT64 translates between them.
